_link.title: I can distinguish between totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent and unipotent stem cells

toLevel2.question: Which type of stem cell can form all cell types including the placenta?

options.explanation: Totipotent cells can form all cell types in the body plus the placenta. Only zygote and morula cells are totipotent.
Pluripotent cells can form almost all cell types but cannot form the placenta.
Multipotent cells can only produce a limited range of related cell types.
Unipotent cells can only produce one type of cell.

toLevel2.question: What type of potency do inner cell mass cells of a blastocyst have?

options.explanation: Inner cell mass cells are pluripotent — they can form almost all cell types but not the placenta (trophoblast).
Inner cell mass cells are not totipotent because they cannot form the trophoblast which develops into the placenta.
Inner cell mass cells have broader potency than multipotent; they are pluripotent.
Inner cell mass cells can differentiate into many cell types, not just one.

toLevel2.question: Which potency level describes haematopoietic stem cells?

options.explanation: Haematopoietic stem cells are multipotent — they can produce many types of blood cells but cannot produce nerve cells or skin cells.
Totipotent cells can form all cell types; haematopoietic cells can only form blood cell types.
Pluripotent cells can form almost all cell types; haematopoietic cells are limited to blood cells.
Haematopoietic cells produce multiple blood cell types, making them multipotent, not unipotent.

toLevel2.question: What can unipotent stem cells do?

options.text: Produce only their own cell type but can still self-renew
options.explanation: Unipotent cells have the lowest potency, producing only one type of cell while retaining the ability to self-renew.

options.text: Produce all cell types in the body
options.explanation: Producing all cell types describes totipotent cells, not unipotent.

options.text: Produce most cell types except the placenta
options.explanation: This describes pluripotent cells, not unipotent cells.

options.text: Produce a range of related cell types
options.explanation: Producing a range of related types describes multipotent cells.

toLevel2.question: How does potency change as development proceeds?

options.explanation: As development proceeds, cells become more specialised and their potency decreases from totipotent to unipotent.
Potency decreases as cells differentiate and become more specialised.
Potency changes throughout development, decreasing as cells differentiate.
Potency follows a clear decreasing pattern as development proceeds.

toLevel2.question: Pluripotent cells can form the placenta.
toLevel2.explanation: Pluripotent cells can form almost all body cell types but cannot form the placenta. Only totipotent cells can form the placenta.

toLevel2.question: The zygote and morula cells are totipotent.
toLevel2.explanation: Totipotent cells are found at the earliest stages of development — the zygote and morula. They can form all cell types including the placenta.

toLevel2.question: {{1}} cells can form all cell types including the placenta, while {{2}} cells can form almost all types except the placenta.
Haematopoietic stem cells are {{1}} because they produce a limited range of {{2}} cell types.
As development proceeds, stem cell potency {{1}} from totipotent to {{2}}.

toLevel3.question: Why are inner cell mass cells classified as pluripotent rather than totipotent?

options.text: Because they cannot form the trophoblast, which develops into the placenta
options.explanation: The key distinction is that totipotent cells can form everything including placental tissue, while pluripotent cells have lost the ability to form the trophoblast.

options.text: Because they can only form one cell type
options.explanation: Pluripotent cells can form almost all cell types, not just one.

options.text: Because they are found later in development than totipotent cells
options.explanation: While true that they appear later, the classification is based on capability, not timing.

options.text: Because they have fewer genes than totipotent cells
options.explanation: All cells contain the same genes; the difference is in which genes can be activated for differentiation.

toLevel3.question: Explain why multipotent cells are described as producing a 'limited range of related cell types.'

options.text: Because they can only differentiate within their lineage, such as blood cells from haematopoietic cells
options.explanation: Multipotent cells are restricted to producing cell types within a specific tissue lineage. Haematopoietic cells produce blood cells but cannot make nerve or skin cells.
Multipotent differentiation is specific to a lineage, not random.

options.text: Because they produce fewer total cells
options.explanation: The 'limited range' refers to the types of cells produced, not the total number.

options.text: Because they can form the placenta
options.explanation: Only totipotent cells can form the placenta; multipotent cells are more restricted.

toLevel3.question: How does the potency hierarchy connect to embryonic development stages?

options.text: Earlier stages have higher potency cells; as cells differentiate through development, potency decreases
options.explanation: Zygote (totipotent) → inner cell mass (pluripotent) → germ layer cells (multipotent) → specialised cells (unipotent). Each developmental stage narrows cell potential.

options.text: All stages have the same potency
options.explanation: Potency clearly changes across developmental stages, decreasing as cells specialise.
Potency decreases, not increases, as development proceeds.
Potency is directly linked to the stage of development and degree of differentiation.

toLevel3.question: Why can unipotent cells still be classified as stem cells despite only producing one cell type?

options.text: Because they retain the ability to self-renew, which is a key property of stem cells
options.explanation: Self-renewal (the ability to produce more of the same stem cell) is a defining property of stem cells. Unipotent cells maintain this ability.

options.text: Because all cells are stem cells
options.explanation: Not all cells are stem cells; stem cells are specifically defined by self-renewal and potency.

options.text: Because they can form any cell type
options.explanation: Unipotent cells can only form one cell type; their stem cell status comes from self-renewal ability.

options.text: Because scientists made an error in classification
options.explanation: The classification is correct; self-renewal defines a cell as a stem cell regardless of potency level.

toLevel3.question: What is the key difference between totipotent and pluripotent cells?

options.text: Totipotent cells can form placental tissue while pluripotent cells cannot
options.explanation: The critical distinction is the ability to form the trophoblast (placenta). Totipotent cells can; pluripotent cells cannot.

options.text: Totipotent cells are larger in size
options.explanation: The distinction is about differentiation capability, not physical size.

options.text: Pluripotent cells can form more cell types
options.explanation: Totipotent cells can form more types (all types including placenta); pluripotent form almost all except placenta.
They differ in their ability to form placental tissue.

toLevel3.question: Explain why potency decreases as cells become more specialised.

options.text: Because differentiation locks cells into specific pathways, reducing the range of cell types they can become
options.explanation: As cells differentiate, genes for other cell fates are progressively silenced, narrowing the cell's potential from totipotent to unipotent.

options.text: Because cells lose DNA as they differentiate
options.explanation: Cells retain all their DNA; it is gene expression that changes, not DNA content.

options.text: Because specialised cells have more organelles
options.explanation: The number of organelles does not determine potency; gene expression patterns do.

options.text: Because older cells naturally lose ability
options.explanation: The loss of potency is due to programmed differentiation, not ageing.

toLevel3.question: Multipotent stem cells can produce any cell type in the body.
toLevel3.explanation: Multipotent cells can only produce a limited range of related cell types within their lineage. For example, haematopoietic stem cells produce blood cells but not nerve or skin cells.

toLevel3.question: Inner cell mass cells are pluripotent, not totipotent, because they cannot form the {{1}} which develops into the {{2}}.
Potency decreases because differentiation {{1}} cells into specific pathways, reducing the {{2}} of cell types they can become.
Unipotent cells are still stem cells because they retain the ability to {{1}}, which is a key stem cell {{2}}.

toLevel4.question: A researcher needs stem cells that can produce any blood cell type but not nerve cells. Which potency level should they select?

options.explanation: Multipotent cells like haematopoietic stem cells can produce a range of related blood cell types but are restricted from producing unrelated types like nerve cells.
Totipotent cells would have more capability than needed and are difficult to obtain.
Unipotent cells only produce one cell type, which is too limited for producing multiple blood cell types.
Pluripotent cells could work but have broader capability than needed, increasing complexity and risk.

toLevel4.question: A student claims that a cell from the morula stage can form a complete organism including the placenta. Is this correct?

options.text: Yes, because morula cells are totipotent and can form all cell types including placental tissue
options.explanation: Morula cells retain totipotency, meaning they can differentiate into any cell type including the trophoblast which forms the placenta.

options.text: No, because morula cells are pluripotent
options.explanation: Morula cells are totipotent, not pluripotent. They retain full differentiation potential.

options.text: No, because only the zygote is totipotent
options.explanation: Both the zygote and morula stage cells are totipotent.

options.text: Yes, but only if the cell is from the inner cell mass
options.explanation: The inner cell mass forms in the blastocyst, not the morula. Morula cells are undifferentiated and totipotent.

toLevel4.question: A patient needs a skin graft. Would totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent, or unipotent skin stem cells be the most practical choice?

options.text: Unipotent skin stem cells, because they directly produce skin cells with minimal risk
options.explanation: Unipotent skin stem cells are already committed to producing skin cells, making them the most direct and lowest-risk option for a skin graft.

options.text: Totipotent cells, because they can form anything
options.explanation: Totipotent cells are difficult to obtain and carry higher risk of forming unwanted cell types.

options.text: Pluripotent cells, because they are most versatile
options.explanation: Greater versatility means higher risk of unwanted differentiation; unipotent cells are more practical for this specific application.
Blood stem cells produce blood cells, not skin cells.

toLevel4.question: Arrange these stem cell types from highest to lowest potency: multipotent, totipotent, unipotent, pluripotent.

options.explanation: Potency decreases in this order: totipotent (all types + placenta), pluripotent (almost all types), multipotent (limited range), unipotent (one type).
Totipotent has higher potency than pluripotent because it can also form placental tissue.
This is the reverse order — from lowest to highest potency.
This order does not follow the correct potency hierarchy.

toLevel4.question: A cell from the inner cell mass is transplanted into a uterus. Could it develop into a complete organism with a placenta?

options.text: No, because it is pluripotent and cannot form the trophoblast needed for the placenta
options.explanation: Inner cell mass cells are pluripotent. They lack the ability to form trophoblast tissue, so they cannot develop a placenta.

options.text: Yes, because inner cell mass cells are totipotent
options.explanation: Inner cell mass cells are pluripotent, not totipotent, and cannot form placental tissue.

options.text: Yes, because all stem cells can form a complete organism
options.explanation: Only totipotent cells can potentially form a complete organism with placenta.

options.text: No, because inner cell mass cells are unipotent
options.explanation: Inner cell mass cells are pluripotent, not unipotent; they can form many cell types, just not placental tissue.

toLevel4.question: A scientist isolates germ layer cells from a gastrula. Classify their potency and predict what they can produce.

options.text: Multipotent — they can produce the cell types specific to their germ layer but not types from other layers
options.explanation: Germ layer cells are multipotent. Ectoderm cells produce skin and nerve tissue, mesoderm cells produce muscle and bone, endoderm cells produce gut lining — each restricted to their layer.

options.text: Totipotent — they can form all cell types
options.explanation: Germ layer cells have already differentiated past the totipotent stage.

options.text: Unipotent — they can only produce one cell type
options.explanation: Germ layer cells can produce multiple related cell types within their layer, making them multipotent.

options.text: Pluripotent — they can form almost all types
options.explanation: By the gastrula stage, cells have differentiated into specific germ layers, reducing potency to multipotent.

toLevel4.question: A medical team needs to grow a new organ from stem cells. Which potency level would be most suitable?

options.text: Pluripotent, because organs contain multiple cell types from different lineages
options.explanation: Organs contain diverse cell types. Pluripotent cells can produce most cell types needed, while multipotent cells would be too limited.

options.text: Unipotent, because organs only need one cell type
options.explanation: Organs are complex structures requiring many different cell types.

options.text: Totipotent, because they are easiest to control
options.explanation: Totipotent cells are actually harder to control and raise ethical concerns.

options.text: Multipotent, because they are most specialised
options.explanation: Multipotent cells are too restricted to produce all the different cell types an organ requires.

toLevel4.question: For a skin graft, {{1}} stem cells are the most practical choice because they directly produce {{2}} cells with minimal risk.
Germ layer cells are {{1}} because they can produce cell types within their layer but not types from {{2}} layers.
Growing a new organ requires {{1}} stem cells because organs contain {{2}} different cell types.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why the potency hierarchy exists in biology rather than all cells remaining totipotent.

options.text: Because decreasing potency through differentiation allows cells to become specialised for specific functions
options.explanation: Organisms need specialised cells (nerve, muscle, blood) with distinct functions. Maintaining totipotency in all cells would prevent the specialisation needed for complex organ systems.

options.text: Because totipotent cells are weaker than other types
options.explanation: Totipotent cells are not weaker; the hierarchy exists because organisms need functional specialisation.

options.text: Because evolution has not had time to fix this limitation
options.explanation: The potency hierarchy is a feature, not a limitation — it enables complex multicellular organism development.

options.text: Because DNA degrades as cells divide
options.explanation: DNA is faithfully replicated during division; potency changes due to gene expression patterns, not DNA loss.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the trade-off between potency and safety when choosing stem cells for medical treatment.

options.text: Higher potency offers more versatility but greater risk of unwanted differentiation; lower potency is safer but more limited
options.explanation: Totipotent and pluripotent cells can form many types but may differentiate incorrectly or form tumours. Multipotent and unipotent cells are safer but less versatile.
Higher potency cells carry greater risk because they can differentiate into unwanted cell types or form tumours.

options.text: Potency has no effect on safety
options.explanation: Potency directly affects risk — more potent cells have more differentiation possibilities, including harmful ones.

options.text: Lower potency is always better for treatment
options.explanation: Some treatments require higher potency cells to produce the needed variety of cell types.

toLevel5.question: Compare the medical utility of pluripotent and multipotent stem cells. In what situations would each be preferred?

options.text: Pluripotent for complex tissue repair needing diverse cell types; multipotent for targeted single-tissue treatments
options.explanation: Pluripotent cells are suited for complex repairs requiring multiple cell types, while multipotent cells are preferred for specific tissue repairs where their restricted potency reduces risk.

options.text: Pluripotent cells are never useful in medicine
options.explanation: Pluripotent cells are valuable for applications requiring diverse cell type production.

options.text: Multipotent cells can replace pluripotent in all situations
options.explanation: Multipotent cells cannot produce the full range of cell types sometimes needed for complex tissue repair.

options.text: Both types are identical in medical utility
options.explanation: Their different potency levels make them suitable for different medical applications.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why induced pluripotent stem cells are significant in the context of the potency hierarchy.

options.text: They demonstrate that potency can be reversed, allowing adult cells to regain pluripotent capability
options.explanation: iPSCs show that the normal decrease in potency is not permanent and can be artificially reversed, opening new medical possibilities without using embryonic cells.

options.text: They prove that potency never changes
options.explanation: iPSCs actually prove the opposite — that potency can be deliberately changed.

options.text: They have no connection to the potency hierarchy
options.explanation: iPSCs directly relate to the hierarchy by reversing the normal decrease in potency.

options.text: They are identical to totipotent cells
options.explanation: iPSCs are pluripotent, not totipotent; they cannot form placental tissue.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the claim: 'Totipotent cells are the best choice for all medical treatments because they can become any cell type.'

options.text: This is incorrect because totipotent cells are difficult to obtain, ethically controversial, and harder to control than more restricted cells
options.explanation: While totipotent cells have maximum versatility, their difficulty of procurement, ethical issues and risk of forming unwanted tissues make them impractical for most treatments.
Maximum potency does not mean maximum suitability; practical, ethical and safety factors must be considered.

options.text: This is correct except for cancer treatment
options.explanation: The limitations of totipotent cells apply broadly, not just to cancer treatment.

options.text: This is incorrect because totipotent cells do not exist
options.explanation: Totipotent cells do exist (zygote and morula), but they are not the best choice for all treatments.

toLevel5.question: Analyse the relationship between the four potency levels and the progressive stages of embryonic development.

options.text: Each developmental stage corresponds to a potency level: zygote/morula (totipotent), inner cell mass (pluripotent), germ layers (multipotent), specialised cells (unipotent)
options.explanation: The potency hierarchy directly maps to developmental stages, with each successive stage showing increased specialisation and decreased potency.

options.text: All developmental stages have the same potency
options.explanation: Potency clearly decreases as development proceeds through each stage.
Potency decreases, not increases, as cells become more specialised.

options.text: There is no relationship between potency and developmental stage
options.explanation: The relationship is direct and well-established in developmental biology.

toLevel5.question: Compare the risks of using pluripotent versus unipotent stem cells in transplant medicine.

options.text: Pluripotent cells risk forming tumours or unwanted tissues; unipotent cells are safer but can only address single-tissue conditions
options.explanation: The broader potential of pluripotent cells includes the risk of incorrect differentiation. Unipotent cells are restricted but predictable.
The risks differ significantly based on potency level.
Unipotent cells are generally safer because their differentiation is more predictable.
All stem cell treatments carry some risk, but the nature of risk differs with potency.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why the concept of self-renewal is important at every level of the potency hierarchy.

options.text: Because without self-renewal, the stem cell population would be depleted as cells differentiate, eliminating the source of new cells
options.explanation: Self-renewal ensures the stem cell pool is maintained even as some cells differentiate. Without it, all stem cells would differentiate and no source of new cells would remain.

options.text: Self-renewal is only important for totipotent cells
options.explanation: Self-renewal is essential at all potency levels to maintain the stem cell population.
Self-renewal is a defining property of stem cells and is critical for maintaining tissue homeostasis.
Self-renewal and differentiation coexist; some daughter cells self-renew while others differentiate.

toLevel5.question: Higher potency stem cells offer more {{1}} but carry greater risk of unwanted {{2}}.
Induced pluripotent stem cells demonstrate that the normal {{1}} in potency can be {{2}} artificially.
